passages.happening:
The widow of one of the sons of the prophets cries out to Elisha. Her husband feared the LORD and is dead, ‘And now his creditor is coming to take my two children as his slaves’ (verse 1). Elisha asks, “Tell me, what do you have in the house?” (verse 2). Nothing, she says, ‘but a jar of oil’ (verse 2).

He tells her to borrow empty jars from all her neighbors, not just a few, then to shut the door behind her and her sons and pour (verses 3-4). They bring jar after jar, and she keeps pouring. When she asks for another, her son says, “There are no more jars” (verse 6), and the oil stops. Elisha tells her, “Go, sell the oil, and pay your debt. Then you and your sons can live on the remainder” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
After chapter 3, where Elisha's word shaped a war between kingdoms, the narrator turns to private wonders. Kings and armies are absent. The people helped are a widow, a childless woman and a community of hungry prophets. While the kings serve other gods, the LORD is keeping faith with the faithful, in their kitchens and their bedrooms. The stories of chapters 4 to 8 are not dated and may be grouped by theme rather than in strict order. They fall in the second half of the ninth century BC.

Israel's law let a creditor take a debtor or his children to work off a debt, but it limited the term and required that they be treated as hired workers, not slaves. For a widow, losing her sons meant losing her only support in old age. Olive oil was used for food, light and medicine, and it could be sold readily.

The miracle is as large as her faith. The oil flows until there are no more jars. It echoes Elijah's miracle for the widow of Zarephath, whose oil did not run out, and it shows that Elisha carries his master's spirit.
passages.later: The law said of a poor countryman, ‘you must not force him into slave labor’ (Leviticus 25:39). Elijah had told another widow, “The jar of flour will not be exhausted and the jug of oil will not run dry” (1 Kings 17:14), and a psalm calls God ‘a defender of the widows’ (Psalm 68:5).
passages.asks: Elisha began with what the widow already had in the house. Ask what small thing you have that God might use. And ask whether your faith gathers only a few jars when God has told you not to.

passages.t: A room for the prophet, and a son
passages.happening:
At Shunem a prominent woman persuades Elisha to eat with her, and after that he stops there whenever he passes (verse 8). She tells her husband, “Behold, now I know that the one who often comes our way is a holy man of God” (verse 9). They build him a small room upstairs with a bed, a table, a chair and a lamp (verse 10).

Elisha wants to repay her. Through his servant Gehazi he offers to speak for her to the king or the army commander. “I have a home among my own people,” she replies (verse 13). Gehazi points out that she has no son and her husband is old (verse 14). Elisha calls her and says, “At this time next year, you will hold a son in your arms” (verse 16). She answers, “No, my lord,” and, “Do not lie to your maidservant, O man of God” (verse 16). But a year later she gives birth to a son, ‘just as Elisha had told her’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Shunem lay on the southern slope of the Hill of Moreh in the Jezreel Valley, a fertile farming region, and the village of Sulam still keeps its name.

The woman calls Elisha holy, qadosh, set apart for God, the word used of God himself as the Holy One of Israel. Her recognition leads her to hospitality, not distance. She builds the holy man a room. Her answer, that she has a home among her own people, means she is secure among her kin and needs no favors from the court.

For a married woman in that world, having no son was a deep sorrow and a threat to her future, since a son would care for her and carry on the family's name and land. She does not ask for one.
passages.later: Long before, the LORD had told Abraham, ‘your wife Sarah will have a son’ (Genesis 18:10), and Sarah laughed. Paul tells the church, ‘Practice hospitality’ (Romans 12:13), and Hebrews says that by showing hospitality to strangers ‘some people have entertained angels without knowing it’ (Hebrews 13:2).
passages.asks: The woman of Shunem gave without asking for anything back. Ask what room you have made in your life for God's work and God's people. And ask what hope you have stopped voicing because you are afraid of losing it.

passages.t: The boy's death, and his raising
passages.happening:
The child grows. One day he goes out to his father among the harvesters and cries, “My head! My head!” (verse 19). A servant carries him to his mother, ‘the boy sat on her lap until noon, and then he died’ (verse 20). She carries him up and lays him on the bed of the man of God, shuts the door, and goes out (verse 21).

She asks her husband for a servant and a donkey, and when he asks why she would go today, she answers, “Everything is all right” (verse 23). She rides to Mount Carmel. When Gehazi meets her with questions, she says again that everything is all right (verse 26). Then she reaches Elisha and clings to his feet. Gehazi tries to push her away, but Elisha says, “Leave her alone, for her soul is in deep distress, and the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me” (verse 27). She says, “Did I ask you for a son, my lord?” (verse 28).

Elisha sends Gehazi ahead with his staff, but the mother will not leave Elisha: “As surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live, I will not leave you” (verse 30). The staff on the boy's face brings no sound. Elisha comes, shuts the door, and prays to the LORD (verse 33). He stretches himself over the boy, and the child's body grows warm. He paces the room, stretches himself out again, ‘and the boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes’ (verse 35). Elisha calls the mother and says, “Pick up your son” (verse 36). She falls at his feet, bows to the ground, then picks up her son and goes out (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
Mount Carmel lay to the northwest of Shunem, a ride of most of a day on a donkey. Her husband's question tells something about worship in the north beyond the royal shrines: the New Moon and the Sabbath were days when people might visit a prophet for worship or teaching.

The story is told with great care and restraint. Her repeated answer, everything is all right, in Hebrew shalom, is both a courtesy and a refusal to speak her grief to anyone but the man of God. Her oath that she will not leave him repeats Elisha's own oath to Elijah in chapter 2. And even the prophet does not know what has happened, because the LORD has not told him.

The raising follows Elijah's raising of the widow's son at Zarephath, with the prophet in an upper room, praying and stretching himself over the child. The staff on its own does nothing. Elisha prays to the LORD.
passages.later: Elijah had raised a widow's son, and ‘the child’s life returned to him, and he lived’ (1 Kings 17:22). Hebrews remembers that ‘Women received back their dead, raised to life again’ (Hebrews 11:35), and the site's notes on Hebrews read it as recalling the two mothers whose sons Elijah and Elisha raised.
passages.hard:
Why did the child die, and what of parents whose children were not given back?

The chapter does not say why the boy died, and it does not blame his mother or anyone else. It records a real loss, a grief that a mother would tell only to the man of God, and a God who answered. Interpreters warn against making this a rule that every loss has a purpose that can be seen, or that enough faith will bring a child back. Most parents who have buried a child were not given that child back in this life, and the Bible does not say they lacked faith. The story's hope reaches further than this one house. Hebrews counts it among the signs of a better resurrection still to come.

The story stays with the mother: her silence, her ride, her clinging, her bitter question. Her grief is not hidden or rebuked, and the prophet says to leave her alone.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The mother said everything was all right while carrying a grief she would tell only to the man of God. Ask where you bring your deepest distress, and whether you have let yourself bring it to God. And ask who near you is saying everything is all right when it is not.

passages.t: Death in the pot, and bread left over
passages.happening:
Elisha returns to Gilgal during a famine. While the sons of the prophets sit before him, he tells his attendant to boil a large pot of stew (verse 38). One man gathers wild gourds from a wild vine and cuts them into the pot, ‘though no one knew what they were’ (verse 39). When the men taste it they cry out, “There is death in the pot, O man of God!” (verse 40). Elisha throws in flour and says, “Pour it out for the people to eat” (verse 41), and nothing harmful is left in the pot.

A man from Baal-shalishah brings twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain. “Give it to the people to eat,” says Elisha (verse 42). His servant asks, “How am I to set twenty loaves before a hundred men?” (verse 43). Elisha repeats the command, for the LORD has said, ‘They will eat and have some left over’ (verse 43). ‘So he set it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of the LORD’ (verse 44).
passages.hearers:
Famine comes up more than once in the Elisha stories. In a farming economy without reserves, a failed harvest could bring hunger quickly, and communities like the sons of the prophets, who seem to have lived with little, felt it first. Gilgal here may again be a town in the hill country. Where Baal-shalishah lay is uncertain, though it seems to have been in the hill country of Ephraim.

The first ripe grain was by law to be brought to the LORD and given to the priests. This man brings it to the prophet instead. Many interpreters suggest that faithful Israelites in the north, unwilling to support the priests of Jeroboam's calf shrines, brought their offerings to the prophets.

The four stories share a pattern: a need, a word or act from the prophet, and a result that meets the need exactly or more than enough. The small gift, offered to the LORD, feeds a hundred, with some left over.
passages.later: The law gave the priests ‘The firstfruits of everything in their land that they bring to the LORD’ (Numbers 18:13).
passages.asks: The servant measured what God could do by what he could see in his hands. Ask where you do the same. And ask what first and best thing you might offer to God, trusting that he can make it enough.
